content.text:
🏗️ Distributed Systems Trade-offs: CAP & PACELC Theorems

In distributed database engineering, system design is fundamentally constrained by network physics and hardware partitioning. System architects must choose trade-offs based on business SLAs and data consistency guarantees.

1. CAP Theorem Breakdown

Formulated by Eric Brewer in 2000, the CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two out of three guarantees when network partitions occur:

  • Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error.
  • Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response without guarantee that it contains the latest write.
  • Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite network messages being dropped or delayed between nodes.

Key Axiom: Because network networks are inherently unreliable (network partitions P are inevitable), distributed systems must trade off between CP (Consistency over Availability) and AP (Availability over Consistency).

2. Beyond CAP: The PACELC Theorem

Proposed by Daniel Abadi, PACELC extends CAP by describing system behavior under normal (non-partitioned) operations:

  • If there is a Partition (P): How does the system trade off Availability (A) vs Consistency (C)?
  • Else (E) under normal operations: How does the system trade off Latency (L) vs Consistency (C)?

3. Database Engines PACELC Classification Table

Database SystemCAP ClassPACELC ClassificationPrimary Architectural Focus
Apache CassandraAPPA / ELHigh write throughput, eventual consistency
MongoDB (Majority Write)CPPC / ECStrong consistency on primary node replica set
Amazon DynamoDBAP / CP ConfigurablePA / EL (Default)Low-latency key-value key distribution

content.text:
💾 Database Storage Engines: B-Trees vs. LSM-Trees

Modern database engines store disk-bound data using distinct data structures optimized for either read-heavy or write-heavy workload patterns.

1. B-Tree Storage Engines (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB)

B-Trees organize data into fixed-size pages (typically 4KB to 16KB) structured as a balanced search tree on disk. Writes update pages in-place.

  • Read Performance: O(log N) point lookups with predictable disk seek costs.
  • Write Overhead: In-place updates require random disk I/O and Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) for durability.

2. Log-Structured Merge-Trees (LSM-Trees, e.g., RocksDB, Cassandra)

LSM-Trees convert random write operations into sequential disk access by buffering writes in an in-memory MemTable and appending updates to a Write-Ahead Log (WAL).

-- SQL Schema Definition Example: Order Transactions
CREATE TABLE order_ledger (
    order_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    user_id UUID NOT NULL,
    amount DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL,
    currency VARCHAR(3) DEFAULT 'USD',
    status VARCHAR(20) CHECK (status IN ('PENDING', 'COMPLETED', 'REFUNDED')),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Create B-Tree index for composite filtering
CREATE INDEX idx_user_orders ON order_ledger (user_id, created_at DESC);

3. Microservices Resiliency: Circuit Breaker Pattern

To prevent cascading failures across microservices, the Circuit Breaker pattern monitors remote service health and trips state transitions when error rates exceed defined thresholds:

  1. Closed State: Requests pass through normally. Successes reset error counters.
  2. Open State: Requests immediately fail fast with a fallback response without calling downstream services.
  3. Half-Open State: A limited probe rate of trial requests is allowed through to test downstream recovery.

"Fail fast, isolate faults, and prevent resource exhaustion across system boundaries."

content.text: Which of the following characteristics apply to LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree) storage engines? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Writes are initially buffered in memory using a MemTable.
Random disk writes are transformed into high-throughput sequential disk writes.
Pages on disk are updated in-place without write-ahead logs.
Background compaction processes merge and deduplicate SSTables.

answer.explanation: LSM-Trees buffer writes in memory (MemTable), convert writes to sequential disk I/O, and continuously run background SSTable compaction. In-place page updates are a characteristic of B-Trees, not LSM-Trees.
